Narrative: During the night shift, a 3rd drilling crew was conducting casing operations (running Ø114.3 mm x 7.4 mm OTTM "E" filter pipes) at a depth of 750 meters using a drilling rig. At approximately 02:50 AM, the crew was handling the 18th filter pipe. After the assistant drillers positioned the pipe into the elevator (Model KM 114-140) and closed the locking handle, the driller began hoisting the block. During the ascent, the elevator's locking handle unexpectedly opened. The pipe was released and fell rapidly onto the rotor area. The falling pipe struck the Machinist, who was positioned on the lower receiving bridge/platform. The victim sustained multiple severe internal and external injuries. Despite immediate emergency calls, the victim passed away while in transit to the medical facility on the highway.
What_Went_Wrong: During the night shift, while hoisting the 18th filter pipe (Ø114.3 mm) to the rig floor, the elevator's locking handle unexpectedly opened. The pipe was released and fell rapidly through the rotor area. The Machinist was standing on the receiving platform below and was struck by the falling pipe.
Corrective_Actions: Strict adherence to Red Zones: Personnel must strictly remain at their designated control posts during hoisting and tripping operations. Any unauthorized movement within the drilling rig area during active operations is strictly prohibited. Exclusion Zone Enforcement: High-risk areas where loads are being moved must be physically barricaded and marked with visible warning signs. Fencing materials must meet safety standards to prevent non-essential personnel from entering the "Line of Fire". Pre-Operation Equipment Verification: Before starting casing or liner running, supervisors and drillers must conduct a thorough inspection of the hoisting equipment, including elevators, to ensure all locking mechanisms are fully functional. Effective Internal Oversight: Formal safety briefings (Toolbox Talks) are insufficient if not supported by active field supervision. Employers must strengthen internal controls to ensure workers follow safety instructions in real-time.

Narrative: On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was released from hospital the same day.
What_Went_Wrong: The 10” gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit, creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
Corrective_Actions: 1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist. 2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible. 3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers. 4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

This incident highlights the importance of ensuring all crew, especially new and existing personnel, are properly trained and aware of steam system risks such as steam hammering, and are competent in following approved operating procedures. Critical equipment including control valves, steam traps, and piping must be maintained in proper working condition and operated in automatic mode where required to prevent condensate build-up and system damage. Adequate temperature and pressure monitoring must be in place and closely observed so that early intervention can be taken during abnormal conditions. Operating procedures must be regularly reviewed and updated to include steam hammering mitigation measures, and the Management of Change (MoC) process must be strengthened to ensure that any system modifications are properly assessed, documented, and reflected in as-built drawings.

Narrative: During the well damping operation by bullheading, the pumping pressure reached the configured limit of the relief valve (hydraulic pop-off) of the mud pump, causing its activation and consequently the failure of the primary well barrier envelope. The opening of this valve was not noticed by the team on board and resulted in the loss of hydraulic pressure on the formation. Furthermore, as monitoring parameters were not fully established, as well as a hidden failure in monitoring the pop-off discharge tank, there was a short delay in closing the valves of the subsea workover assembly and Surface Flow Tree (secondary Well barrier envelope), allowing the migration of gas through the production column and DPR (Drill Pipe Riser), reaching the tank room (100% LEL) through the relief valve and, subsequently, discharge on the main deck of the unit through the air exhaust system of the storage room tanks, covering a significant extension of unclassified area (peak of 64% LEL on the sensor close to the well testing plant).

Narrative: On 8 October 2025 on an offshore rig, a lifting operation was underway to land an 11.8 m, 2.67 ton bottom hole assembly (BHA) into a storage basket on the riser deck. During the final positioning, the BHA made a sudden uncontrolled movement. The forward end either contacted the basket edge, rotating the load toward the injured person, or the crane made an unintended movement. The injured person was positioned in a narrow space between riser guide posts with no escape route available. He had earlier climbed onto adjacent baskets and manually guided the load several times to open covers in the inner basket. The BHA struck him in the chest and compressed him against another basket. Emergency response was immediate, and medical evacuation was carried out via search and rescue (SAR) helicopter. The investigation identified multiple human, organisational, technical, and task-related contributors including lack of hands-free lifting, trainee crane operator without supervision, congested deck layout, communication challenges, inadequate planning, and procedural non-compliance.
What_Went_Wrong: Hands-free lifting methods were not used despite being available, exposing personnel to the line of fire. The crane was operated by a trainee without required mentor supervision, contrary to procedure. The lift was treated as a routine task, and risk assessment did not account for congested deck layout, lack of escape routes, basket orientation requirements, or blind zones for the crane operator. The BHA was landed the wrong way due to missing communication, partly caused by language barriers. The deck was heavily congested, forcing the injured person into restricted and hazardous positions to open basket covers and guide the BHA manually. No exclusion zone was established. Several crew members were new in roles or on the rig, and norms for intervening or stopping unsafe work were inconsistent. Organisational follow-up on competence, planning quality, and supervision responsibilities was insufficient. These factors created multiple error traps and eliminated critical barriers.
Corrective_Actions: Lifting operations involving heavy BHA components require detailed planning that reflects actual deck conditions, special equipment requirements, and correct use of hands-free practices. Exclusion zones and escape routes must always be established and maintained. Trainee crane operators must only operate under direct mentor supervision in accordance with formal competence requirements. Communication expectations with third-party vendors must be clear, including language-barrier mitigation. Deck layout planning between logistics and lifting operations must 27 EUROPE ONSHORE ensure safe accessibility, visibility, and controlled load movement. Stop-work authority must be reinforced culturally to empower all personnel to intervene. Competence verification prior to mobilisation and clearer integration of procedures into workflow are essential to prevent recurrence.
